citeinfo.title: The North American Freshwater Migratory Fish Database (NAFMFD): Characterizing the migratory life histories of freshwater fishes of Canada, the United States, and Mexico

descript.abstract: We developed the North American Freshwater Migratory Fish Database (NAFMFD) that synthesizes current knowledge of migratory status, pattern, and behavior for native and non-native freshwater fish species throughout North America, including 1,241 species representing 79 families and 322 genera.
descript.purpose: This information on species’ migratory life histories will aid researchers in addressing threats to migratory fishes including habitat fragmentation. Our approach can provide guidance for developing similar databases in other regions. Collectively, this work offers new insights into the range of freshwater fish migratory life histories, stimulating a need to better understand this diversity globally.

procstep.procdesc: We began by developing a list of freshwater fish species to form the database using published freshwater fish species lists. Our first list included species listed in Jelks et al. 2008. We then added species compiled by Daniel et al. 2015.

We assigned status, patterns, and behaviors to fish species in the database. For each fish species, we reviewed published books focused on freshwater migratory fishes and freshwater fish life histories in regions of North America, including Canada, Mexico, and the United States. We used GoogleScholar for our literature search because it provides results for both peer-reviewed journal articles and gray literature. Literature searches were conducted using a fish species name and combination of keywords including: “life history”, “life cycle”, “ecology”, “migratory”, “migration”, “movement”, “mobile”, “diadromy”, “anadromy”, “catadromy”, “amphidromy”, “potamodromy”, “non-migratory”, “non-mobile”, and “sedentary.” We integrated all information included in the Global Register of Migratory Species (Riede 2004) for those species that migrated long distances, and if information on a species’ life history was not documented in peer-reviewed literature or gray literature, we referred to FishBase and the IUCN Red List.

We standardized the information compiled for fish species using the following data categories and assigned descriptors to each species. The term status refers to the general migratory life history of the species. This includes whether a species is migratory or non-migratory or if it is suspected to migrate. It also includes whether it displays distinct migratory and non-migratory populations or individuals within a population. Finally, the term status includes whether the migratory life history could not be determined based on an absence of information (i.e., undetermined). If the species was determined to have a migratory status, we proceeded to assign a pattern. Pattern refers to the separate habitats that a migratory fish uses in their life cycle which can include saltwater and freshwater habitats (i.e., diadromous) and/or wholly freshwater habitats (i.e., potamodromous). If the species was diadromous, we assigned one or more of the following behaviors to the species, which indicates the timing and direction of a migration of a life stage between separate habitats: anadromous, semi-anadromous, catadromous, semi-catadromous, and amphidromous. We did not define behaviors for potamodromous species because specific behaviors are difficult to define or are not well known for most potamodromous fishes. We assigned a fish species a suspected migrant status if we were able to find information on the migratory life history of a species but could not determine the specific pattern for the species. Species with distinct migratory and non-migratory populations or populations comprised of migratory and non-migratory individuals were assigned both a migratory and non-migratory status. If species were found to not migrate from our review (i.e., a source clearly indicated that the species was not migratory), the species was assigned a non-migratory status. If we could not find any statement on the migratory life history of a fish species, we assigned the species an undetermined status.

We compiled the status, pattern, and behavior assignments for each freshwater fish species into a single database with each row containing information for one species; sources used to assign information were also included (see list of sources in Appendix S1 in Supporting Information). Species taxonomy was obtained from the Integrated Taxonomic Information System (ITIS 2021; https://www.itis.gov/), with database columns representing family, scientific, and common names along with family, genus, and species ITIS codes. Columns representing status, pattern, and behavior are marked as binary (0/1) for each species with 1 indicating a species exhibits a particular migratory status, pattern, and behavior while 0 indicates it does not. Subsequent columns in the database identify the sources for the status, pattern, and behavior for a species, with cells containing the status, pattern, and behavior as text (e.g., non-migratory; potamodromous; anadromous) identified from a specific source.

Sixteen reviewers with expertise in North American freshwater fishes verified the status, pattern, and behavior assigned to each fish species in the database. Experts included university researchers and government and non-governmental scientists. Experts reviewed species according to regional knowledge.
